title: Generate Content: Written Content
summary: Written Content is the text-focused part of Generate Content: phishing lures, fraudulent financial communications, fabricated job adverts, forged employment credentials, decoy documents, and the persona text that sustains a false identity over weeks or months. Authorship may be manual, outsourced, or AI-assisted, and AI is typically used to localise wording into a target's language and to mimic the register of a trusted sender. The distinguishing property is that the text contains no malicious code, so content filtering that hunts for payloads sees nothing unusual. Detection therefore rests on identity and context: authentication results for the claimed domain, display-name and address mismatches, first-contact patterns between two organisations, and requests that deviate from the sender's historical behaviour, such as a change of bank details or an out-of-band payment. Useful artefacts include mail headers and message trace records, file metadata on attached documents, and similarity across messages sent to many recipients.

beginner.definition: Written content is the text an attacker prepares to support a trick. It can be a phishing email, a fake invoice, or a false job advert. It can also be a forged reference letter, or posts on a fake social profile. It may be typed by a person or produced with help from an AI tool. It is only words, so it carries no harmful code.
beginner.whyItMatters: People trust documents and messages that read well. A well-written request can persuade a finance team to pay a fake invoice. It can also persuade a recruiter to share private data. Because the text looks like normal business writing, technical filters often allow it through. If nobody checks who really sent it, the message reaches the inbox and the fraud succeeds.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers names, job titles, and writing habits from websites and social media.
They pick a request that fits the target's daily work, like a payment or a document review.
They write the message, and may use AI to fix grammar and match the target language.
They copy logos, signatures, and formats from real company documents to add credibility.
They send the text by email, chat, or a fake profile, sometimes to many people at once.
They reply quickly and politely to keep the victim engaged until the request is done.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where everyone splits the bills. A note appears on the kitchen table. It has the landlord's letterhead and the correct account number format. A polite line asks for this month's rent by Friday. Nobody thinks to call the landlord, because the note looks exactly like his usual letters. The words did the work, and no lock was touched.
takeaways: Well-written text can carry an attack without any malicious file attached.
Compare the sender address and domain with the name shown, not just the display name.
Treat unusual payment or data requests as suspicious even when the writing is polished.

objectives: Describe how written content differs from its parent technique, Generate Content.
List the common forms of written material used in social engineering campaigns.
Explain how AI-assisted tools change the speed and quality of fabricated text.
Identify the mail header and message trace artefacts that reveal a forged sender.
Explain why payload-based filtering fails against text-only lures.
